topic: What if you could grow at will?
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
GROW AT WILL?

power.rule: one word, and you get bigger, as big as you like
power.look: a gold pulse from the feet, eyes lit gold, a height ruler climbing to ×10, a GROW chip; a low swell snapping up into a springy overshoot

length_note: Long cut of the formula for a 16:9 YouTube upload of at least a minute: all seven beats, with the fun and the turn played out.

script.text: Mum hid the cookies on top of the fridge. Grow. Snack time.
Late for school? Grow. One giant step.
Your best friend is looking for you. Grow. Again. Again. Okay, that's terrifying.

script.beat: 2 the premise and its rule (title card)
script.text: What if you could grow, any time you wanted? One word, and you get bigger. As big as you like.
Sounds amazing. Pigeons think you're a building. Your best friend gets the best seat in town. And you're the coolest kid in the city.

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact, worked out
script.text: But here's the catch. Ten times taller means a thousand times heavier. Your bones? Only a hundred times stronger. So every square inch of bone carries ten times the load. And a human thigh bone breaks at about ten times your body weight. Your very first step? Snap. That's real.
You sit down on a rooftop and wait to shrink back.
The next morning, a man in a suit is waiting in your kitchen. He has a photo of you. And an offer.
Then the ceiling starts to crack. Upstairs, your little sister just said the word.

script.beat: 7 cliffhanger, a question for the comments
script.text: Do you run up and save her… or do you keep your secret?

science.claim: Ten times taller means a thousand times heavier.
science.working: Scaling a body by 10 in height, width and depth multiplies its volume, so its mass at the same density, by 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000. Pip is about 1.5 m tall: at x10 he is 15 m, a 4 to 5 storey building, as the rooftop shots show.
science.source: Square-cube law: Galileo, Two New Sciences (1638); J. B. S. Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size' (1926), the giants Pope and Pagan, ten times as high as Christian and a thousand times his weight.

science.claim: Your bones are only a hundred times stronger; every square inch of bone carries ten times the load.
science.working: A bone's strength in compression goes with the area of its cross-section: at x10 that area is 10 x 10 = 100 times larger. So each square inch carries 1,000 / 100 = 10 times the weight it did.
science.source: J. B. S. Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size' (1926): the cross sections of the giants' bones were only a hundred times Christian's, so every square inch of giant bone had to support ten times the weight.

science.claim: A human thigh bone breaks at about ten times your body weight; your very first step, it snaps.
science.working: Haldane: the human thigh-bone breaks under about ten times the human weight. Standing, a x10 giant already loads his bones at ten times their usual stress; a step adds the load of walking, so the thigh breaks at the first step. Haldane concludes the giants would have broken their thighs every time they took a step, which is why they sat down in the picture he remembered (hence Pip sitting on a rooftop).
science.source: J. B. S. Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size', 1926.
